summary:
NASA’s SPHEREX photographs the whole sky every six months, in 102 infrared colors. But each image is a 65 MB scientific file. Normal people can’t open that.

So we built Mira: a free public observatory for SphereX that runs in your phone browser.

Type a name or RA/Dec, hit play, and watch 27 years of NASA pictures flip by: 2MASS, WISE, then every SphereX visit. MIRA measures what moved and how fast, draws spectra on the fly and tracks brightness, with Gaia and WISE overlays and NASA’s quality flags.

AI points you to the movers: a scout network that searched the whole sky, plus Meta’s V-JEPA 2, fine-tuned on our examples.

Does it work? Yes.

epsilon indi b: 4.70″/yr (Gaia says 4.68)
blind test: 92% of known movers found, zero false alarms
202,528 claims re-measured on raw SphereX images → 17,604 moving stars confirmed
635 aren’t in Gaia or SIMBAD. Open now for anyone to check.

SphereX’s data was always public. Mira makes it usable by the public.

The sky is changing. Now anyone can watch.
details:
what it does

ok so. Mira is a public web observatory for NASA’s SPHEREx. three parts.

1. the lab. this is the thing the challenge asked for.
type a name or RA/Dec. one time bar plays that patch of sky through 27 years of NASA pictures: 2mass (1999), WISE (2010), then one deep SPHEREx image per visit.

it answers four questions:

  • what moved?
  • how fast?
  • what does its light say? (a 0.75–5 µm spectrum, computed on the fly. methane gets detected automatically.)
  • did it brighten or fade?

plus the tools you’d want: adjustable field of view, Gaia + WISE overlays, NASA’s quality flags, all 102 bands, six detector co-adds, coordinates in the URL, embeds, and CSV / FITS / python exports.

2. the sky + space maps.
sky = the whole sky on one time bar. watch SphereX fill it in on the real dates of its 1.6 million exposures. the planets where they are tonight. “my sky now” for your own horizon.
Space = a 3D model of the Sun’s neighborhood, with real stars.

3. a verified catalogue.
39.9 billion wise detections → 1.56 million claims of motion. we re-measured 202,528 of them on raw SphereX exposures. 17,604 moving stars confirmed.

how it works!!

there’s no data server. none.

a tiny index lists which exposures cover each patch of sky. your browser grabs only the piece of each 65 MB file it needs (under 1 MB), straight from NASA’s public archive. then it aligns the image, applies NASA’s flags and measures.

every visit is tied to Gaia using the field’s own stars. and “moved” means 5 sigma. not vibes.

does it work??

yep. we checked it against stars everyone already knows:

  • epsilon indi b: 4.70″/yr (Gaia: 4.68)
  • barnard’s star: 10.46 (Gaia: 10.39)
  • WISE 0855: 8.21 (published: 8.15)

then a blind test on 459 fields: it found 92% of known movers, and zero false alarms across 5,757 still stars.

AI

  • a small world model forecasts a field, right in your browser.
  • a scout network, trained on a GPU cluster, searched the whole sky. of its 400 strongest new marks, 393 are known fast movers. so it knows what it’s looking at.
  • Meta’s v-JEP A2, fine-tuned on our examples, gives a second opinion.
  • an AI assistant, powered by K2 Horizon, explains the page and runs the instruments for you. it only uses numbers the instruments actually computed. no making stuff up.

benefits + impact

  • anyone curious: works in a phone browser. no install. no account.
  • classrooms: students measure a star’s motion on NASA’s own images and check it against Gaia. no telescope needed.
  • citizen scientists: 635 confirmed movers that neither Gaia nor SIMBAD lists. one click away. same idea as NASA’s Backyard Worlds.
  • researchers + mission teams: measurements with errors, exports, an open API, embeddable views.

and here’s the part we love: running mira costs about US$150 a year. so US$488 million of SphereX’s public data can reach literally everyone.

tools

  • languages: typescript, python
  • site: react, vite, three.js (3D), aladin lite (sky maps), uPlot (charts), webgl
  • pipeline + training: astropy, numpy, scipy, pytorch
  • hardware: a GPU cluster for the all-sky survey and AI training. laptops for everything else.
  • deployment: docker, nginx, caddy, plus one script that re-indexes each new spherex release
  • data: nasa spherex, 2mass, wise, allwise, catwise2020, jpl horizons. esa gaia DR3. cds simbad + vizier.
  • AI coding assistants: claude code wrote and reviewed much of the code under our direction, with codex and antigravity as reviewers. every use is logged.

what’s creative

spherex is hard to blink.

its pixels are 6″. it rolls between visits. every exposure sees a different color. so a perfectly still star flickers.

mira turns that mess into a steady film: three surveys on one time bar, every visit tied to Gaia.

and it’s a real scientific instrument that runs entirely in your browser, on raw NASA files, with no server.

what we considered

  • accessibility: phone first. plain words before numbers. “explain it to me” on every panel.
    • blends within one pixel get flagged, not judged.
    • SphereX alone sees motions above about 2.5″/yr.
    • Planet Nine as proposed is too faint for SphereX. the detection limits tool tells you what each field rules out.
    • AI marks are places to look. not discoveries.
